events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Maya proposes Maya, Omar. I'll include myself to show confidence in the opening team and pair with Omar, who gave a thoughtful read in the early exchange — a solid trust-building start for Mission 1.

I want to stand by this proposal. Mission 1 with just two seats is already a tight squeeze — one wrong pick and the whole thing collapses before we even get a foothold. Omar and I communicated well in the early exchange, and I think pairing two players who are actively engaging from the start sets a good tone for trust. I'd rather go with people I've already seen reason with clearly than gamble on someone who hasn't spoken up yet. I'm open to hearing what the rest of you think, but I'd encourage Elena, Felix, and Priya to weigh in soon — if there's a concern about either of us, now's the time to raise it before we lock in a vote.

I'm a Loyal Servant, so I'll be plain about my position: I have no private information, no hidden reads, and nothing clever to contribute — my value here is purely in how I reason about the vote. With five players and a two-person team on Mission 1, a single bad pick ends our run immediately. That makes this the highest-leverage vote of the game, and it means the burden of proof sits on the names on the table, not on the names left off it.

On Maya and Omar: Maya's reasoning was that she wanted to pair with someone who showed thoughtful engagement in the early exchange, and she's taken herself along to put skin in the game. That's a defensible instinct. A leader who includes herself gives the rest of us a stake in the outcome instead of asking us to trust a team she's insulated from. I don't want to relitigate a proposal over style.

But I want to be honest about the limit of what I can verify. Omar, I haven't heard your reasoning yet — you haven't had a turn in this discussion, and I have no information about your alignment beyond what you say here. Can you tell me directly why you think you belong on a two-person mission team, and specifically what you think you can contribute to the team going forward if this mission succeeds? I'm not accusing you of anything; I'm asking because I am asked to approve a team where one misread costs us the entire game, and your argument is the part of this decision I haven't heard.

If Omar's answer convinces me, I vote yes for Maya and Omar. If it doesn't, I'd rather hear from Elena and Priya and consider swapping a name — but I'd need an actual reason, not a vague feeling, and I've heard one argument so far (Maya's) and it holds up reasonably well. I'd rather approve a team I understand than block one and hand leadership to a player who might propose something worse.

Felix, I can't prove my alignment through an opening speech. My case is simply that I know I'm Good and will play Success, so from my perspective this team needs only Maya to be Good. If it succeeds, I'd use the result alongside the votes and subsequent proposals—not treat it as proof that both of us are trustworthy, since Evil can play Success. Also, a failed first mission is a setback, not an immediate loss; Evil needs three failed missions.

I strongly advise against approving this team. Felix, you noted that the burden of proof is on the table, but neither Maya nor Omar has provided anything concrete. Maya's justification rests on vague early-game rapport, and Omar's response—while composed—is completely unfalsifiable. Anyone, Good or Evil, can say they will play Success.

Approving the very first proposal on Mission 1 is rarely in Good's interest when we have seen zero voting patterns and have up to five attempts to gather information. If there is Evil on this team, we are blindly handing away the mission without learning anything from the table. Rejecting gives us a voting record to analyze and allows leadership to rotate so we can evaluate different combinations.

Priya, we haven't heard from you yet. What is your read on Maya pairing herself with Omar right away, and do you feel comfortable approving this team rather than seeing another proposal?

Elena, thanks for pulling me in — here's my honest read. I don't share your enthusiasm for rejecting this team, and I want to explain why without pretending to have information I don't have. Like Felix, I'm a Loyal Servant with no private reads, so all I can offer is reasoning.

First, on your argument that rejecting gives us a voting record: approving a team also produces a voting record. Every player's ballot is revealed either way, so rejecting doesn't buy us information we can't get by voting yes. What rejection actually buys us is safety — the mission doesn't go out — at the cost of rotating leadership and burning one of our five proposals. That's a real trade-off, but it's not free, and with a two-person Mission 1 team, a success would tell us a lot about both Maya and Omar going forward.

Second, on Maya's proposal itself. I put weight on the fact that she put herself on the team. Evil leaders sometimes self-select, sure, but a leader who includes herself is staking her own credibility on the result, and if this mission fails, Maya is the first person we scrutinize. That's a coherent structure for assigning blame later, and I'd rather have that than a leader sending two other people into the fog.

Third, on Omar's answer to Felix. I agree with Elena that 'I know I'm Good and will play Success' is unfalsifiable — anyone can say it. But I'll note that Omar didn't oversell it. He explicitly told us not to treat a success as proof, and he flagged that Evil can play Success. That kind of calibrated honesty is worth something, even if it's not proof of anything. What I noticed, though, is that Omar answered the easy half of Felix's question and skipped the hard half. Felix asked two things: why you belong on this team, and what you'd contribute going forward if it succeeds. We only got the first part.

So, Omar, directly: Felix asked what you think you can contribute to the team going forward if this mission succeeds, and I'd like to hear that answer before I lock in my vote. Concretely — what's your plan for how we should read votes and proposals on Missions 2 and 3 if Maya and Omar come back clean? I'm not asking you to prove your alignment; I'm asking because a two-person team on Mission 1 is the highest-leverage decision on the table, and the forward-looking half of your case is the part none of us has heard.

If your answer is substantive, I'm currently leaning yes on Maya and Omar — Maya's self-inclusion plus a coherent plan from Omar is enough for me to gamble one mission rather than start burning proposals. If it's another restatement that you'll play Success and nothing more, I'll side with Elena and vote to see a different combination.

Priya, if this team succeeds, I'd start Mission 2 with Maya and me plus one of the three who sat out, but I wouldn't treat the success as proof: an Evil player can deliberately play Success. I'd compare the revealed votes with each player's stated reasons, then examine who gets proposed as the third member and why. A rejection of this team isn't inherently suspicious, and neither is approval.

For Mission 3, a two-person team gives us a chance to test a combination against the Mission 2 result. If Mission 2 fails, I'd look carefully at the added player but also keep Maya and me under scrutiny; we couldn't know who played Fail. If both succeed, that's useful evidence, not a guarantee, and I'd still compare it with the proposals and votes before choosing the next pair.

Elena, I hear your concern, but I think your rejection argument cuts both ways. You say approving this team blinds us — but a rejection on Mission 1 doesn't blind us to anything either. As Priya pointed out, both approval and rejection produce a voting record. What rejection actually gives us is leadership rotation, and I'd ask everyone: what do you gain from handing the next proposal to a different leader when the core question is the same — who do you trust on a two-person team?

Omar addressed Felix's question with genuine reasoning about how he'd analyze future missions, and Priya confirmed that his forward-looking answer was substantive. That's exactly what I was looking for from my teammate. He didn't oversell himself, he didn't ask you to take his word as proof, and he laid out a concrete framework for reading votes and proposals going forward.

I put myself on this team deliberately. If Mission 1 fails, I'm the first name on the chopping block. That's not the play of someone hiding behind others — it's someone willing to stake their credibility on a partnership they believe in. The alternative is burning a proposal to chase a hypothetical better combination we haven't even seen yet.

I'm asking you, Felix and Priya, to vote yes. Elena, I'd genuinely like to know: what team would you rather see on Mission 1, and what specifically makes it stronger than this one?

Maya, to answer your question: I would rather see a team that doesn't immediately form a self-reinforcing duo on proposal 1. If this proposal fails, leadership passes to me, and I would look to field a team with Felix or Priya—players who have approached this opening discussion with genuine analytical caution rather than mutual back-patting. Look closely at what just happened here. Maya and Omar are actively pushing to lock this in before even hearing Priya's reaction to Omar's second statement, with Maya already asserting on Priya's behalf that Omar's answer was substantive. More critically, Omar's stated plan for Mission 2 is to carry both himself and Maya forward plus one other player. Approving this team does not just risk Mission 1; it hands them an immediate narrative claim to two of the three seats on Mission 2. Felix, you noted earlier that the burden of proof sits on the table and that you wanted to see Omar's forward-looking plan before deciding. Now that Omar has explicitly stated he intends for the two of them to form the core of Mission 2 as well, are you genuinely comfortable handing that kind of leverage to proposal 1 without seeing a single alternative proposal?

Elena, you put a direct question to me, so let me answer it straight: yes, I'm comfortable approving Maya and Omar — but not because Elena's concern is wrong, rather because I think it proves less than it appears to.

First, the leverage argument. You're right that Omar stated an intention to carry Maya and himself into the core of Mission 2. But an intention is not authority. The Mission 2 team is proposed by the Mission 2 leader, and Maya is the one who proposed this team and who will be the one to put names in front of us next. If she wants a different pairing on Mission 2, she proposes a different pairing. Omar's plan constrains nobody — it only constrains Omar. What approving this team actually does is put Maya and Omar on the hook if Mission 1 fails, which is the opposite of what you described: the risk lands on them, not on the rest of us.

Second, on your alternative. You told us you'd field a team with Felix or Priya — but you haven't named a pair, and you haven't said what that pair is better at doing than Maya and Omar on a two-person Mission 1. "Players who approached the discussion with analytical caution" is a compliment about conversation style, not a reason to believe someone will succeed on a mission card. If you'd reject on the grounds that we haven't seen a second proposal, I'd note that Priya already made the counter: both approval and rejection produce a voting record, and rejection costs us one of five proposals while rotating leadership to you. I think Elena's case is that the trade is worth it — I'd like to hear that trade defended as a trade, not assumed.

What I won't do is treat a rejected first proposal as free information. It isn't free; it burns a proposal, and it hands the next team to a player who hasn't yet demonstrated a better one.

Third, on my own condition. I said I'd want Omar's forward-looking plan, and I got it. It was specific and calibrated — he'd compare revealed votes against stated reasons, he'd examine who gets proposed and why, and he explicitly refused to treat a success as proof. I also appreciate that he didn't oversell it. Felix and Priya have both heard the same answer I have, so I won't relitigate it.

Maya, one direct question, since you're the one holding the revision: if you think Elena's argument about a Maya-and-Omar core on Mission 2 is genuinely compelling, would you use your one revision to swap Omar for Priya or for Elena — and if not, what makes the Omar pairing the stronger bet on a two-person team? I want to know whether the Maya-Omar pairing is a considered commitment or a default before I put my ballot down.

Felix, direct answer to your question: no, I wouldn't use my revision to swap Omar for Priya or Elena, and here's why the Omar pairing is the stronger bet on a two-person team.

First, on Omar himself. He's already demonstrated exactly the kind of reasoning I want in a teammate. He answered your forward-looking question with a concrete framework, he explicitly refused to let a success be treated as proof, and he flagged that Evil can play Success. That calibration is rare in an opening game — most players oversell or underdeliver, and Omar did neither. If I'm staking my credibility on this team, I want the person beside me to reason the way Omar reasons.

Second, on swapping for Priya or Elena. I have no specific reason to trust either more than Omar on a mission team, and I'd be swapping known reasoning for unknown reasoning. Priya and Elena have both made thoughtful contributions in discussion, but discussion quality and mission reliability aren't the same thing. Omar has engaged substantively when pressed — twice now — which is more than I can say about the alternative swaps.

Third, on Elena's concern about the Mission 2 core. Elena raised a fair point about narrative leverage, but as you yourself noted, intentions don't constrain anyone — proposals do. If this mission succeeds, I'll propose whatever team I think is strongest on Mission 2, and that might or might not include Omar. What matters right now is Mission 1, and on a two-person team the pairing needs to be tight. I put myself on this team because I'm willing to be scrutinized if it fails, and I paired with Omar because he's shown me the reasoning I trust.

I'd rather commit to a considered pairing than hedge with a swap I can't justify. That's why I'm keeping the team as-is.

Third and final turn from me, so let me make my position explicit and then put one specific question to you, Elena.

My vote is yes on Maya and Omar.

Where I land, briefly, on everything still open:

On your leverage argument: Omar's Mission 2 plan is an intention, not authority. The Mission 2 team is proposed by the Mission 2 leader, and Maya is proposing on Mission 1 — so the naming rights are Maya's, and her own e12 statement says she may or may not carry Omar forward. What approving this team actually does is put Maya and Omar on the hook if Mission 1 fails. That is the opposite of granting them a protected narrative core.

On the two-person risk: Felix here has no private reads, so I reason from structure. A two-person Mission 1 team means we learn the most from a clean result and lose everything from a bad one, which argues for a pair whose joint behavior is actually observed — and we have observed Maya and Omar's, twice each, under direct pressure. Maya self-included, which puts her credibility on the line. Omar gave a calibrated forward-looking plan and explicitly refused to treat a success as proof. That combination is what I want on a two-seat card.

On the cost of rejection: it burns one of five proposals and rotates leadership to a player who has not yet named a team. I've said this already and I won't repeat it, but it belongs in my final statement — a rejected first proposal is not free information, and both outcomes produce a revealed voting record either way.

Now the question, Elena, and it is a specific one, not an invitation to argue in circles: you said you would rather field a team of your own, and you gestured at "Felix or Priya" but never named a pair. So name it — the exact two players you would propose for Mission 1, and the one concrete reason that pair is more likely to succeed on the card than Maya and Omar. If you have a reason, I will weigh it honestly, and if it's good enough I will reconsider my ballot. If what you have is a preference for avoiding a self-reinforcing duo rather than a positive case for a specific pair, then I'll go ahead and vote yes on Maya and Omar, because I would rather approve a team I can explain than reject one on the strength of an alternative nobody has actually specified.

That's my last word either way, and I'm glad to hear you out before the ballots are cast.

Felix, you asked for the exact pair and the concrete reason: I would propose myself and Felix. First, following your own principle, including myself puts my own credibility and skin in the game—if it fails, I am entirely accountable. Second, unlike Omar, you have approached this proposal with genuine critical inquiry rather than defending an unearned mutual-protection pact. Maya and Omar have moved in lockstep from turn one, and approving them gives two players who back each other unconditional leverage.

Priya, you specifically stated in your previous turn that you were leaning yes only if Omar gave a substantive, forward-looking plan, and that you would vote to see a different combination if it fell short. In turn e8, Omar's concrete proposal for Mission 2 was simply to carry both himself and Maya forward into two of the three seats. Does an answer that presumes their duo should automatically anchor the next mission genuinely satisfy what you asked for, or does it justify taking a second proposal to see an alternative?

Elena, you asked me directly whether Omar's e8 answer genuinely satisfies the condition I set, or whether it justifies a second proposal — so let me answer that precisely, because my vote follows from it.

My condition in e7 had two parts. I said I'd lean yes if Omar gave a substantive forward-looking plan for how we should read votes and proposals on Missions 2 and 3, and I said a mere restatement of 'I'll play Success' would send me to your side of the table. What Omar delivered was not a restatement. He gave a concrete framework: compare revealed votes against each player's stated reasons, examine who gets proposed as the third member and why, treat the Mission 2 and Mission 3 results as evidence to be weighed against proposals and votes rather than proof, and keep Maya and himself under scrutiny if anything goes sideways. That is a real analytical plan, and it was specific to the question Felix actually asked. So on the letter of my own stated condition, yes — it satisfies it.

Now, the part of your challenge that has force: Omar did presume that he and Maya would anchor Mission 2. I acknowledge that openly. But I weigh it against three things. First, an intention binds no one — Maya is the Mission 2 leader if this proposal passes, and she has already said on the record that she may or may not carry Omar forward. The presumption is a data point about Omar's mindset, not a grant of authority. Second, Omar explicitly paired that presumption with a commitment to keep himself and Maya under scrutiny if results are ambiguous — that is not the language of someone building an unaccountable power bloc. Third, and most importantly: approving this team puts Maya and Omar on the hook, not the rest of us. If Mission 1 fails, they are the two names we scrutinize first, and Maya volunteered for that position when she self-included.

On your alternative — you and Felix — I'll be honest that I find it no stronger than what's on the table. You name critical inquiry as your qualification, but Felix would be swapped in on the strength of one speech's tone, exactly the kind of unverifiable quality you objected to in Maya's case for Omar. And rejecting costs us one of five proposals and hands leadership forward without any of us having seen a mission result.

So my answer to your question is: yes, it satisfies what I asked for, and I'm voting yes on Maya and Omar. I want to be clear that I'm doing this on the record, against my own stated conditions, so that if this mission fails, my yes vote is part of the evidence about me too. Maya and Omar have earned this vote; I'm willing to stake a mission on that.

Maya confirms Maya, Omar. I've heard every voice on this table and I'm keeping the team as Maya and Omar. Felix laid out a clear case for approving, Priya confirmed Omar's forward-looking plan met her stated condition, and Elena's alternative of herself and Felix — while honest — doesn't offer a stronger pairing for a two-person mission than a self-including leader paired with someone who's reasoned calably under pressure twice. This team stands.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (2 fail cards).

Elena proposes Elena, Felix, Priya. Mission 1 failed with 2 fail cards, which mathematically confirms both Maya and Omar as the two Evil players in a 5-player game. That leaves Elena, Felix, and Priya as the confirmed Loyal Servants, making this the only viable and clean 3-player team.
The two Fail cards establish that Maya and I are Evil. Elena's proposed team is the only three-player team without either of us, so I won't pretend there's a credible reason to change it.

Omar's already said he won't change the team, and I won't either — Elena's proposal of Elena, Felix, and Priya is the only clean play. The math is what it is: two fail cards on a two-person team confirms Omar and me as Evil. I'm not going to waste anyone's time fighting arithmetic I can't dispute.

What I want to put on the table now is what happens after this mission succeeds. Missions 3 through 5 will require teams that include identified Evil players — the structure of the game forces it. That means we'll face a choice the same way every game does: which Evil player goes on which team, and with whom.

Felix, you've been this table's most disciplined reasoner — you called the burden of proof early, you set conditions before approving Mission 1, and you stuck to them. When Mission 3 arrives and the team must include me or Omar, what framework will you use to decide which of us earns a seat, and who else you'd want alongside? I'd rather hear your answer now than when the pressure is on, because the quality of that reasoning will matter more than anything said today.

Elena's team of Elena, Felix, Priya is the only clean team available, and I want to state my reasoning plainly before the ballots.

Mission 1 failed with two Fail cards on a two-person team. Two Fail cards cannot be played by a single player — only one Fail is needed to sink a mission. So both Maya and Omar played Fail, and they are confirmed as the two Evil players. That leaves Elena, Felix, and Priya as the three Loyal-side players, and this proposal is the only three-person team without either of them. I see no reason to spend any further deliberation on it; the only thing worth debating is what happens on Missions 3 through 5, where the structure of the game forces at least one Evil player onto every team.

Maya asked me earlier what framework I would use when that moment comes, and I'll answer on the record rather than wait. My framework: the only decision that matters is which pair of the confirmed Good players accompanies which Evil player, because each Evil on a team needs a chance to fail it, and each Good on that team is a hostage. I will judge by stated positions and past behavior, not by reputation: Maya self-selected onto the first team and anchored it with Omar, and Elena has now shown the opposite profile — she asked for concrete pairs, pressed for reasons, and reversed course only when the evidence forced it. Where those two profiles conflict, I'd rather not spend a Good seat next to the player who has already demonstrated a coordinated bloc with the other confirmed Evil player.

On accountability: Maya, you and Omar each had the chance to fail that mission and both of you took it, and the group paid for it. That is on the record and I won't pretend otherwise. But the blame for Mission 1 does not transfer to the players who are sitting out and taking this mission cleanly, and I'd ask that this vote be judged on the math rather than on the grudge from the last round.

I vote yes on Elena, Felix, Priya. And I'd rather we spend our remaining discussion energy planning Mission 3 well than relitigating Mission 1, which is settled.

Elena's team — Elena, Felix, Priya — is the only proposal that survives the arithmetic, and I'm voting yes without reservations. Two Fail cards on a two-person mission means both Omar and I played Fail. I won't dress that up as anything else, and I won't burn a rejection on the one team nobody at this table can honestly question.

Felix, your Mission 3 framework singled me out. You said you'd rather not spend a Good seat next to the player who has already demonstrated a coordinated bloc with the other confirmed Evil player. I want to push back on that, because it draws a distinction where none exists: Omar and I proposed the same team and approved it together — the bloc was symmetric. What differs is what came after the result. I conceded the arithmetic in my first turn of this discussion, accepted that Mission 1's failure lands on my shoulders first, and I'm putting myself forward now: if Mission 3's two-person pair must include one of us, I would rather be the Evil seat you choose deliberately than have the choice treated as unprincipled.

So here's what I'd hang my own vote on later, and you're the Mission 3 leader: on what basis will you choose between me and Omar, given that your own stated framework can't distinguish us? And if your answer is "neither — I'll pair two confirmed Good players," I'd ask you to defend that too, because you told this table yourself that the structure of the game forces at least one Evil player onto every remaining team. A Good-only Mission 3 would contradict the position you just staked.

Yes to Elena, Felix, Priya — the only team without a confirmed Evil player, and no one has grounds to challenge the arithmetic.

But I need to correct something I said last round, because Maya's question rests on it: I claimed the game structure forces at least one Evil player onto every remaining team. In a five-player game that is wrong, and being wrong about it matters. We are three confirmed Good — Elena, Felix, Priya. Mission 3 needs two players, Mission 4 needs three, Mission 5 needs three. Every one of those can be filled entirely from our three names. We do not need to seat Maya or Omar even once.

Why that is the right path: our only win condition is three successful missions, followed by the Assassin's guess. A single Fail card on any of the remaining missions kills that path permanently — a failed mission hands Evil a second fail toward their three, and no combination of the remaining missions then gives us three successes. So every mission we put an Evil player on is a mission we might lose the game outright. Seating Maya or Omar buys us nothing; their presence turns a guaranteed success into a coin flip on whether the mission fails at all.

So to answer Maya directly, on what basis would I choose between you and Omar: I no longer have one, and I want to be honest that the answer changed when I realized my earlier premise was false. If we were ever forced to seat one of you, the fallback is Maya — on the narrow ground that you proposed and led the Mission 1 team while Omar followed, and the agenda-setting player is the easier one to keep away from naming later teams. But that is a fallback for a situation I do not expect us to create.

On Mission 1: two Fail cards means both of you played Fail. Nothing about intention, calibration, or reputation changes that, and I won't relitigate it.

Priya, one specific point for you: do you agree we should plan to field all-Good teams on Missions 3, 4, and 5, and do you see any reason to seat either Evil player before the assassination phase?

Felix, you asked me directly, so here is my answer: yes, I agree we should plan to field all-Good teams on Missions 3, 4, and 5, and I see no reason to seat either Maya or Omar before the assassination phase.

The arithmetic Felix laid out is correct and I want to confirm it on the record. We are three confirmed Good players and the remaining team sizes are two, three, and three. Every remaining mission can be filled entirely from Elena, Felix, and me. Seating a confirmed Evil player converts a guaranteed success into a gamble on their mission card, and a single Fail card anywhere along the way ends our path to three successes. There is no compensating benefit. Evil needs two more fails; handing them a seat with fail potential on every remaining mission is exactly how we lose.

I want to address Maya's framing directly, because I think it deserves a clear response. Maya argued that the Mission 1 bloc was symmetric and asked to be treated as the principled choice for a future Evil seat. But the premise of that entire negotiation is one we should simply decline. This is not a question of which confirmed Evil player has been more gracious in defeat. Maya and Omar both played Fail on a two-person mission — that is settled. The relevant point now is that a confirmed Evil player lobbying for inclusion on future teams is not a gesture of cooperation; it is a request for the opportunity to fail a mission. Granting that request would be indefensible regardless of how reasonably it is argued, and I want to be explicit that I won't be moved by appeals to fairness between the two of them. There is no Evil seat to allocate.

So my position going forward: Elena, Felix, and I take every remaining mission. I'm voting yes on this proposal, and I intend to vote yes on any proposal containing only the three of us for the rest of the game.

My vote is yes on Elena, Felix, Priya, and I'll keep it brief because there is nothing left to argue about this proposal.

Two Fail cards on a two-person mission cannot come from one player — one Fail is enough to sink a mission — so Maya and Omar are both confirmed Evil. That leaves Elena, Felix, and Priya as the three Loyal-side players, and this is the only three-person team in the game that contains neither of them. Any other proposal either includes a confirmed Evil player or is too small for Mission 2. Rejection would burn a proposal and produce the same forced outcome on the next round, since we have no alternative clean team to rotate to. There is no trade-off here to weigh; there is only the correct proposal.

Maya asked earlier in the discussion whether we should treat her as the principled choice for a future Evil seat, and Priya answered that squarely, and I agree with that answer. A confirmed Evil player arguing for inclusion on future teams is not requesting cooperation; it is requesting another chance to place a Fail card. We are three confirmed Good with remaining team sizes of two, three, and three — Missions 3, 4, and 5 can all be filled from our three names alone. Every mission we seat Maya or Omar on converts a guaranteed success into a coin flip, and one Fail anywhere permanently kills our path to three successes, because a failed mission hands Evil a second fail toward their three and no combination of remaining missions then yields three successes. There is no compensating benefit to seating either of them, and there is no Evil seat to allocate.

So my position for the rest of the game is straightforward: Elena, Felix, and Priya take every remaining mission. We do not need to seat either confirmed Evil player even once, and we should not. If a later leader proposes otherwise, that proposal should be rejected on this same arithmetic, not on reputation or on how gracefully either of them argues for a seat.

Elena, Felix, and Priya — approved. That's my second turn and my position is settled; I don't expect to have anything further to add unless someone proposes a team that seats Maya or Omar, in which case I'll want the floor again to explain why that trade is a bad one.

My vote is yes on Elena, Felix, and Priya. I've already stated my position clearly over the last two turns — two fail cards on a two-person mission is definitive, and this is the only clean three-player team available. I won't belabor the point further.

What I'll note is that Elena, Felix, and Priya should use this remaining discussion time productively rather than repeatedly reconfirming what everyone at this table already agrees on. The real strategic decisions come on Missions 3 through 5, and how the three of you coordinate leadership rotation and team composition will determine whether this game ends in three successes or stalls. Every redundant reassurance burns a turn that could be spent planning ahead.

I'm voting yes and I have nothing further to add on this proposal unless someone objects to the only team on the table.
Elena confirms Elena, Felix, Priya. Keeping the proposed team of Elena, Felix, and Priya as it is mathematically confirmed to be the only all-Good team.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Felix proposes Felix, Priya. The arithmetic is settled: Mission 1's two Fail cards on a two-person team confirm Maya and Omar as the two Evil players, leaving Elena, Felix, and Priya as the three Loyal side. Mission 3 needs only two players, so the optimal and essentially forced choice is a pair drawn entirely from our three confirmed Good — seating Maya or Omar would turn a guaranteed success into a coin flip on their card for no benefit. I include myself to take direct accountability for the proposal and to keep ownership of the naming rather than delegating it. Priya joins me because she has been the most consistently disciplined reasoner at this table — she set explicit conditions, held Omar to them, and reversed her own standard only when the evidence forced it — and because she also carries the point that a confirmed Evil player lobbying for a seat is requesting another chance to place a Fail card, which is the principle I want embodied in the team. Elena sits out this mission only because the size constraint requires one Good player to sit; she returns on Mission 4 and Mission 5, where all three of us can be seated and no Evil is ever required. If a later leader proposes anything containing Maya or Omar, that proposal should be rejected on this same arithmetic, not on reputation.

Felix and Priya are a clean team, so I have no credible objection to the proposal.

Elena, before Mission 1 you preferred yourself and Felix over Maya and me. What specifically led you to choose Felix over Priya at that point?

Omar, that is straightforward and already reflected in the Mission 1 discussion: Felix had spoken up with active skepticism and demanded justification from your pairing, whereas Priya had indicated she was leaning toward approving your proposal. Naturally, I looked to partner with the player showing the most analytical caution on the record at that moment.

Regardless, the current situation is entirely clear. Felix and Priya are both confirmed Loyal, and this two-player proposal is mathematically guaranteed to succeed. I support the team.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
